s2.p1: A little ahead of time, let us introduce the concept of a **global object**.
s2.p2: A **global object** is the environment in which we "live" (operate) and beyond which we cannot go.
s2.p3:
On the client side JS works in the browser, in the console of which, by the way, we perform all the operations below.

This is possible because the **V8** engine built into each browser interprets our code and executes it.
s2.p4: Simplistically speaking, the **global object** for us is the browser (more precisely, its **object model**, but we will deal with that later).
s2.p5: The browser itself works in the operating system and has access to its capabilities.
s2.p6: But we cannot go outside the browser and interact with the operating system directly.
s2.p7: So, the operating system allocates system resources, in particular memory, for the work of applications, including the browser.
s2.p8: The browser manages the memory resource allocated to it, part of which it allocates to the **V8** engine.
s2.p9: Next we will talk about variables, i.e. the memory that will be used by our application.
s2.p10: For our code, access to the global object is provided by the **⟦f0⟧** variable.
s3.p1: Memory is a huge number of cells, each of which can contain 0 or 1.
s3.p2:
Such a cell is a **bit** of memory.
That is why the binary number system was the basis for the first computers.
The **8 bits** make **1 byte** of memory.
s3.p3: A maximum of 8 units can be placed in **1 byte** of memory, i.e. the binary number 11111111.
s3.p4: In decimal notation this would be the number 255 without a sign.
s3.p5: If **byte** (8 bits) is interpreted as a signed number, one bit will contain the sign of the number (**+ **or** -**), so the maximum number with a sign that can ‘fit’ into one byte is 127 (seven units).
s3.p6: ^^Any number can be represented in binary by a set of zeros and ones:^^
s3.p7: ^^Any number can be decomposed by powers of two + remainder (0 or 1).^^
s3.p8: ^^Since in binary, a two is a ten, we replace the powers of two with the powers of ten, add up, and add the remainder.^^
s3.p10: As you have already guessed, the computer can only work with binary numbers, i.e. sets of zeros and ones.
s3.p11: The reasonable question is how does the computer store text, pictures and videos, etc.
s3.p12: Any shade is represented as several numbers:
s3.p13: Any character is represented by its code (number):
s3.p14: Thus, any information is represented in computer memory by sets of zeros and ones, and managing memory allocation is a very complex process.
s3.p15: It is quite improbable to operate on physical memory addresses to access data.
s3.p17: You don't need to know the physical addresses where your data will be stored.
s3.p18: You need to come up with a name for each data item, and tell the engine what data item you will store under that name.
s3.p19: This is how a **variable** is created.
s3.p20: So, **variables** make it easier for you to manipulate your data and keep your operating system and running applications safe.

s4.p2: In order for the engine to correctly interpret this set of zeros and ones, it must know what was stored at the given address: a number, a string or something else.

s4.p8: ^^Variables can store numbers, strings, logical values, specific **⟦f1⟧** and **⟦f2⟧** values, as well as **reference type** data, which we'll get to later.^^
